title: Keeping Small Languages Alive
context:
A. Linguists estimate that around half of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today may disappear before the end of this century, which means that, on average, one falls silent every few weeks. Violent suppression is now a less common cause than economic calculation. Parents who live in minority communities frequently decide that their children will have better chances of finding jobs and doing well at school if they learn a dominant national or international language, and so they stop speaking the older one at home. Within a single generation, a thriving tongue can become one that only grandparents remember.

B. One of the most successful responses has been the language nest, a pre-school in which elderly fluent speakers spend the whole day talking to very young children exclusively in the heritage language. The first nests were set up by community volunteers in the 1980s, without waiting for official support, and they spread rapidly because families could see the results. By the time the children reach primary school they can understand their elders and manage in two languages, something classroom lessons for older learners rarely achieve.

C. Documentation offers a different kind of protection. Linguists record the voices of the last remaining speakers, compile dictionaries and write down traditional stories, creating archives that may be useful for centuries. Many specialists, however, warn that a recording is not the same as a living language: a language that exists only on a hard drive cannot be used to joke, argue or tell a child to come home. Ethical questions also arise. In some communities, certain words may be spoken only during ceremonies, and elders insist that the community, not the researcher, must decide who can listen to the recordings.

D. Technology can help, but it also reveals new obstacles. Smartphones and keyboards are designed for large languages, so speakers of small ones often find that the letters or accents they need are missing and give up writing messages in their own tongue. Volunteers have therefore designed new keyboards and free apps that teach vocabulary through games. Perhaps more important, teenagers in several communities now share jokes and music videos online in the minority language, showing that it can sound modern and fun rather than old-fashioned.

E. A few languages have been revived after losing their last native speakers, usually by learning from old texts and recordings. Revivals face an unusual problem: a language that stopped being used decades ago has no words for mobile phones or climate change. Committees must invent them, often by combining old roots or borrowing from relatives of the language, and disputes are common. Purists want new vocabulary to follow traditional patterns, whereas pragmatists prefer whatever younger speakers will actually accept and use.

F. How should success be measured? Counting speakers is misleading if they are all elderly, so many experts focus on whether children learn the language from their parents, which they regard as the decisive sign of health. Practical support matters too. Laws granting a language official status oblige public bodies to offer services in it, and employers who use it in the workplace give young people a reason to keep it. Yet funding for such measures is often short-term, depending on the priorities of whichever government is in power.
